1-01.text: Every day in Hong Kong, about four people die of liver cancer.

1-02.text: Here, it's one of the three deadliest cancers, alongside lung and colorectal. And it's not just us. Worldwide, it's the sixth most common cancer, and the third deadliest.

1-03.text: Here is the thing. We already have medicines. Just not good enough.

1-04.text: The study we follow calls it a huge unmet need.

1-05+1-06+1-07.text: So, why not just make a better one? Because that's way harder than it sounds. Like, ten-to-seventeen-years hard.

1-08.text: Start the search the year we were born, and it might only be ready now. It can cost almost 2.8 billion US dollars. And of drugs tested in people, only about one in ten reaches the market.

1-09.text: To see why, let's follow one drug's journey. Every medicine walks the same road. Find a target. Find a hit, a first molecule that works on it. Improve it. Test it in cells, then animals. Then human trials. Phase one, two, three. Then approval. Any step can fail.

1-10.text: Now, here's where it gets interesting. In 2024, part of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, for AlphaFold, an AI that predicts the shape of proteins.

1-11.text: So, can AI walk the first step faster? Let's follow one real case, where AI tools took on liver cancer. And part of it starts right here, in Hong Kong.

2-01.text: Hong Kong first. In 2011, a team at the Chinese University of Hong Kong studied liver tumours from patients at the Prince of Wales Hospital. One protein kept showing up raised. CCRK, also called CDK20. Fast forward to 2023. An AI drug-discovery study goes after the same protein, with co-authors at Insilico Medicine's Hong Kong office in Science Park.

2-02.text: So our research question is, how can computer-aided methods help scientists find and assess potential cancer drug candidates?

2-03.text: And we will answer it with one case study, CDK20 in liver cancer.

2-05.text: One, to identify the major computer-aided methods used in cancer drug discovery. Two, to evaluate how these methods help scientists assess potential drug candidates.

2-06.text: So how did we check all this? We read. A lot. No lab work of our own. This is a literature review. At the centre, one original study by Ren and colleagues in Chemical Science, 2023, with its supplementary data. Around it, the earlier Hong Kong study, papers behind two AI tools, a 2023 review, a textbook chapter, and a 2026 expert Perspective, which we read only as an abstract. Around it, the earlier Hong Kong study, papers behind two AI tools, a 2023 review, a textbook chapter, and a 2026 expert Perspective, which we read only as an abstract. Around it, the earlier Hong Kong study, papers behind two AI tools, a 2023 review, a textbook chapter, and a 2026 expert Perspective, which we read only as an abstract. read only as an abstract.

2-07.text: For everyone's source, we asked, what kind is it, how much did we read, and how strong is the evidence? Who did the work? Were there controls and repeats? One thing worth knowing, most authors of the main study work for Insilico Medicine, which built its AI tools. They say so openly. Useful evidence, not an independent check.

2-08.text: So here's where we're going. First, the lock. Then how AI helped cut a key for it. Then what happened in the lab. And finally, the big one. How much did the computers really help?

3-01.text: Okay, to get this, picture a lock and a key.

3-02.text: Inside your cells, proteins do a lot of the work. Most drugs grab one protein tightly and change what it does, slotting into a pocket like a key into a lock.

3-03.text: Scientists call the lock the target, and the key a candidate molecule. A good key fits its own lock tightly, and opens no one else's. That's called selectivity.

3-04.text: Our lock is CDK20. It's an enzyme, a protein with a chemical job. Its keyhole is a pocket where it normally grabs a small molecule called ATP. Plug that pocket with the right key, and the enzyme can't do its job.

3-05.text: Why this lock? Remember the Hong Kong team. In 36 of 52 liver tumours, CDK20 was higher than in nearby non-tumour tissue. High levels went with later-stage tumours and shorter survival. And turning CDK20 down in liver cancer cells slowed their growth.

3-06.text: So, it is a really strong suspect, not only cause of liver cancer, but a lock worth trying.

3-07.text: In 2023, an AI platform called PandaOmics backed that hunch. It combed ten liver cancer data sets, over a thousand tumour samples and hundreds of healthy ones, plus research papers. People checked its top 20 by hand, and CDK20 came out on top, with no approved drug against it yet.

3-08.text: And no one had measured CDK20's shape. That takes a lot of hard lab work, and only a small fraction of proteins have ever been measured. Without a 3D shape, even computer predictions of binding get expensive, slow and difficult.

3-09.text: So, you've got a lock nobody can see. How do you cut a key in the dark?

4-01.text: The team did something that once sounded like science fiction. They asked an AI to guess the shape. Imagine a protein as a string of beads that folds into a 3D shape. The order of the beads is the sequence. AlphaFold learned from known structures how sequences fold. Give it one, and it predicts the shape, plus how sure it is about each part.

4-02.text: This was the first time AlphaFold had been used to find a hit like this.

4-03.text: But look closer. One end of the protein, a floppy tail, had really low confidence. And in the model, it lay across the keyhole, with one building block sitting inside the ATP pocket. Trust it blindly, and you'd cut keys for a blocked door.

4-04+4-05.text: So what did they do? They cut the tail off. The AI made the guess. A human caught the problem.

4-06.text: And every single round in a real lab costs time and money.

4-07.text: Generative AI takes that loop and moves this into a computer. The platform here, Chemistry42, runs dozens of AI models side by side, built on known chemistry. They invent new molecules for this exact keyhole, score them, learn from the scores, and go again. Its makers say it turns out new structures within hours.

4-08.text: AI didn't replace the scientists. It just ran their trial and error inside a computer, at light speed.

4-09.text: the team gave it the pocket's shape and one rule every key must grip a spot called the hinge its filters are built to toast designs with reactive or possibly toxic groups and to score how drug-like and easy to make each one is

4-10.text: It came back with 8,918 brand-new designs. Way too many to make. So each key gets tried in a virtual lock. That's docking. The computer predicts how a molecule might sit in the pocket, and scores the fit. Similar designs get grouped, 54 make the shortlist, and chemists pick just seven to make.

4-11+4-12.text: So the computer picked the winners? Not quite. A docking score is a clue, not proof. Only the lab can tell.

5-01.text: So, the moment of truth. Seven real molecules, made in a real lab. Do any actually grab CDK20? Grip is measured as Kd. Roughly, how much molecule it takes to grab half the protein. Lower means tighter.

5-02.text: Six of them barely held on. But one of them stood out. Its name? 001.

5-03.text: The clock read just 30 days, from picking the target to this first confirmed hit.

5-04.text: But then came a second test. Because grabbing a lock isn't the same as jamming it. Does 001 actually stop CDK20 from working? That's measured as IC50. How much you need to cut the enzyme's activity in half? For 001? Above 6,000 nanomolar.

5-05+5-06.text: The key went into the lock. But it barely turned. So was that it? Back to square one?

5-07.text: Not at all. This is where the loop kicks in again, now with real lab data inside. The results went back in, with a predicted pose of how 001 sat in the pocket. Sixteen new designs. Six made and tested. All within 30 days of that first hit.

5-08.text: And one of them, 048, grabbed about fifteen times tighter. Then the enzyme test. Remember, 001 needed more than 6,000 nanomolar. 048 needed just 33.4.

5-10.text: Then, the big step, living cells. After three days with 048, Huh7 liver cancer cells, packed with CDK20, lost half their living-cell signal at about 210 nanomolar. Comparison cells, HEK293, needed about 1,700. Roughly eight times.

6-01.text: So, the big question. How much did the computers actually help? Let's line up before and now.

6-02.text: See the lock. Before, hard lab experiments, and without a 3D shape, design was expensive, slow and difficult. Now, a free prediction, downloaded from a public database.

6-03.text: Finally, a hit. Before screening real compounds by the millions, an approach a 2023 review says has hit a costly bottleneck. Now, 8,918 designs inside a computer, and just 13 molecules actually made.

6-04+6-05.text: Millions of compounds screened before. Here? Thirteen made. Thirteen. That's honestly wild.

6-06.text: Before, a ten-to-seventeen-year road, with finding a hit just the opening stretch. Now, 30 days to the first hit, and a better key within another 30.

6-07.text: Before, every change meant another costly lab round. Now, a predicted picture of the first key guided sixteen designs, and the grip got about fifteen times tighter.

6-08.text: To be fair, these pairs come from different studies, they compare scale and speed, not one race run side by side. But the paper itself calls the work cost- and time-efficient.

6-10.text: So, where's 048 on the road? Target? Found. Hit? Found. Improving it? Started. Cells? First tests, done. Animals and clinical trials? Not yet.

6-11.text: Here's what the end of that road can look like. Some AI-assisted cancer drugs have walked much further. In September 2026, one of them, lirafugratinib, was approved in the US for a bile duct cancer. Others failed along the way. And 048? Its makers chose not to take it to trials, and shared it with other researchers instead.

6-12.text: 048 is at the very start of the road. But for this case, that start took weeks, not years.

7-01.text: So what should happen next? We'd suggest three things.

7-02.text: 1. Walk 048 further. It's public now, so anyone could try. Test it in more liver cancer cells and normal liver cells, then animals, and check how the body handles it and what else it hits. The authors had already listed these steps.

7-03.text: 2. Check the AlphaFold model against a lab-measured structure, once one exists. And feed every result, including the failures, back into the next round.

7-04.text: 3. Race them. An AI route and a classic route, same target, same budget, same definition of a hit. Then we'd know exactly how much faster AI really is.

8-01.text: So back to where we started.

8-02.text: How can computer-aided methods help scientists find and assess cancer drug candidates? In this case, at four points. Picking a target from data. Predicting the lock's shape. Designing new keys. And ranking which ones to make. That's our first objective, met for this case.

8-03.text: And our second? These methods helped the team assess candidates fast. Screening by the millions became thirteen molecules made. And on a road measured in years, the first hit came in 30 days, and round two made the key turn.
